en: The Buddha’s Teaching on the Contemplation Sūtra:
Contemplating the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. Regarding the practice of recollecting and contemplating the Buddhas of the ten directions: while seated, one contemplates the eastern direction.
A vast, brilliant light appears, and there is seen only a single Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), raising his hand to preach the Dharma. One focuses the mind...
Clearly observe:
the marks and signs of radiance are as clear and distinct as if written in glowing light.
Constantly bind this to the mind so that external conditions do not distract it.
If other thoughts arise, one should collect the mind and bring it back.
Seeing in this manner, the vision increases until ten Buddhas appear; one then sees ten Buddhas, and as it increases further, one sees a hundred Buddhas.
From as few as a thousand Buddhas up to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas—
if they are near, they immediately become distant and vast.
One sees only the lights of all the Buddhas interconnecting.
When the mind is clear and one observes until this state is attained,
one further visualizes the southeast direction in the same manner as the previous visualization.
Once this has been accomplished, it extends as far as the western direction;
indeed, it is likewise so for all ten directions.
Having thus turned toward each direction, one sees the Buddha in every place.
He preached the Dharma appropriately.
Furthermore, at one time he went to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions;
in a single thought-moment, he perceived them all throughout their entirety.
One who has accomplished the concentrated mind sees the Buddhas of the ten directions within meditative absorption;
they all preach the Dharma for them, whereby their net of doubts is entirely removed and they attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If there are those who, due to the causal conditions of past karma, do not see the Buddhas,
they should repent during the six periods of the day and night.
By means of exhorting, requesting, and rejoicing, they will gradually come to see the Buddha.
"Even if the Buddhas do not preach the Dharma for them,
these people will attain peace and happiness and be free from all afflictions.
The *Sūtra on the Essentials of the Five Gates of Dhyāna* says:
The Essential Methods for Sitting Meditation consist of five gates:
first, ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing);
second, aśubha (contemplation of impurity).
Third, the mind of loving-kindness;
fourth, contemplation of conditions;
fifth, mindfulness of the Buddha.
The two gates of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) and *aśubha* (impurity),
and the gate of contemplating conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—
these three gates have both internal and external objects of focus.
The mindfulness of the Buddha takes the compassionate mind as its object toward external realms.
As for the five gates, they are taught according to the illnesses of sentient beings;
if one has much distractedness of mind, one is instructed in ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing).
If one has excessive greed for sensory experience, they are instructed in the contemplation of impurity;
if one has excessive anger, they are instructed in loving-kindness;
if one is excessively attached to a self, they are instructed in dependent origination.
If the mind does not subside, instruct them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
they should then contemplate the Buddha with single-minded focus.
When contemplating the Buddha, they must do so with a sincere heart.
Contemplate the marks and signs of the Buddha until they are clearly distinguished; having done so,
close your eyes and maintain the recollection within your mind.
If it becomes clear, then open your eyes;
observe it with the utmost clarity of mind,
and thereafter return to your seat.
With body upright and mind focused,
as before, as if facing the true Buddha,
one should be clear and distinct, no different from the reality.
He immediately said to his teacher,
"Focusing one's mindfulness to see the Buddha is no different [from seeing it directly].
The teacher said:
Return to your original seat, fix your mindfulness upon the crown of your head, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
At that time, an image of the Buddha will appear upon your crown;
from one to ten, and even to infinity.
If the practitioner sees many Buddhas emerging from the forehead,
and if they depart far from the body before returning, this indicates that one is a person of the Mahāyāna.
The Buddhas manifested by those of the three vehicles likewise cause the ground near their bodies to turn golden;
all these Buddhas level the terrain until it is as smooth as the palm of a hand.
Pure as a mirror,
one contemplates one’s own body as luminous and pure as the earth;
this is called the realm of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (nienfo sanmei).
Having attained this state, one says to the teacher:
"This is a favorable state.
This is called the contemplation of the initial gate.
Furthermore, now fix your attention in your mind.
Then, upon contemplating the Buddha, you will see all Buddhas;
they emerge from the mind, holding lapis lazuli staffs in their hands.
They emerge from both ends.
The light-flames of those of the Three Vehicles vary in size.
Having thus emerged, the subsequent Buddha grasps the staff.
He remained standing upright with his mind focused;
finally abiding as a Buddha,
he turned his body and re-entered.
First, one goes to the limit of extinction (*nirodha*) and then returns to follow after people.
If it is a person of the Hīnayāna, they stop once they have entered extinction.
If it is a person of the Mahāyāna, having already entered [extinction], [they continue].
From every pore of his body, [light] filled the four seas,
extending upward to the Summit of Existence and downward to the limits of the wind.
Having thus manifested this clarity, they return to human form, appearing like pure lapis lazuli.
The reason the radiance returns to the human body is to demonstrate the realm of leaping, surging, vigor, and swiftness.
The marks and signs are thus as previously stated by the Master.
This is called the "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
They are named foundations of mindfulness because they are able to give rise to all meditative concentrations (samādhi).
This is the certainty of the staff of the heterodox path;
the light of the marks is the mark of wisdom.
This is the sphere of the ordinary person within [the mundane realm].
Furthermore, he causes [the practitioner] to abandon the previous two contemplations and fix the mind upon the navel.
Thus, with single-mindedness, he contemplates the navel; after contemplating the navel for a short while, he perceives that the navel has a sign of movement.
Observing with undistracted attention,
he saw an object at his navel that resembled a hawk’s egg.
Its color was a fresh white.
He then addressed his teacher once more,
and the teacher said:
You should further observe the locations;
you will then see that there are already lotus flowers,
with stems made of lapis lazuli.
A platform made of gold;
upon the platform is a Buddha,
seated in the full lotus posture.
The first Buddha is like the navel;
there is further a lotus flower,
and upon it is another Buddha.
They sat cross-legged;
thus they emerged one after another in succession,
until they reached the shore of the great ocean.
The last Buddha re-enters the navel of the second Buddha;
the second Buddha re-enters the navel of the third Buddha.
In this manner, they successively re-enter one another until they reach the navel of a human being.
The Buddha commanded that for each individual Buddha,
lotus flowers emerge from the pores of the practitioner’s own body once they have entered the practitioner’s navel.
Filling the entirety of space like hanging jeweled necklaces,
such lotus flowers were produced.
It enters completely into the navel;
the practitioner’s body then becomes supple and soft,
and he experiences a sense of lightness and joy within himself.
His own body became bright and pure, with a color like that of various jewels.
He immediately informed his teacher, who said:
This is the sign of the attainment of the Great Wholesome Samādhi.
Furthermore, he causes [the practitioner] to observe the navel;
immediately, five auspicious signs are seen upon the crown of the head.
Having observed this, one sees a Buddha sitting cross-legged within a light;
observing further, one sees that the Buddha possesses something.
He then saw various lotus flowers emerge from the Buddha’s mouth;
having emerged, they filled the entire earth.
He further beheld the Buddhas within the five lights.
He saw five lions emerge from his navel; having emerged,
they ate [the lotus] and produced a lotus flower,
which then returned into the five-colored light.
Once the lion has entered the Buddha’s navel, five rays of light [emerge], and the Buddha immediately enters this crown-mark; this is the meditative sign of the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*.
When the practitioner beholds these lights entering the Buddha’s body, the practitioner becomes golden in color.
Having seen a thing within the navel,
as bright and pure as the sun or moon,
he informed his teacher upon seeing it.
The Master said:
"If you observe further, you will see the Buddhas.
From beneath his armpits and from his waist, he manifested four ordinary Buddhas in total.
Then, as each Buddha emerged, they emitted immeasurable rays of sunlight.
The sunlight was bright and pure;
by means of this sunlight, one could perceive the forms of the four continents.
Above reaching the Peak of Existence and below reaching the limit of wind,
all were clearly perceived without exception.
To see things as clearly as if they were in the palm of one's hand, without any obstruction,
is called pure liberation.
Having seen this, one again sees four buddhas;
they emerge from the place of entry as if entering it,
and having entered, one again sees a flame-like radiance.
Entering from the front and exiting from the back;
entering from the back and exiting from the front;
exiting from the left and entering from the right.
Exhaling through the right and inhaling through the left,
one thus eventually sees one's own body as luminous and pure,
as well as the water on all four sides as a perfect circle of pure light.
This is called the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
it belongs to the realm of the fourth dhyāna.

To practice the method of the visualization of white bones: first, one contemplates that the skin, flesh, tendons, and veins of the body all completely decay until only the white bones remain connected.
The color is like white jade or snow, and its light is likewise.
If one does not see it,
they are like a person suffering from leprosy.
The physician said,
"He must drink blood that is the color of milk, and then he will recover.
His family members had a silver vessel made to hold the blood and ordered him to drink it.
He said, "Your illness has been cured.
The patient replied,
"I shall not eat blood."
The saying goes:
"White milk—
do you dare not see what is within it?"
"Are they all white?
It is because of your own transgressions that you see them as blood.
Simply conceive of them as milk."
Do not harbor thoughts of blood.
After seven days, it will thus transform into milk.
How much more so when it is actually white bones that one cannot see?
One then sees the person as bone; within each person made of bone, the arising and ceasing of the mind continues in succession like beads strung on a thread.
What is seen in this manner, as well as the contemplation of the external body, is likewise.
If one applies the mind with diligence and does not slacken,
it is like seeing smoke when drilling for fire.
When digging a well, one sees mud;
it will not be long before water is found.
If the mind is tranquil, then while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one will see white bones everywhere.
It is clearly understood to be like water that has settled:
when clear, one sees the face;
when turbid, one does not see it.
The Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha: The Buddha is the Dharma King;
he is able to cause people to attain various kinds of wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, those who practice seated meditation should first bring the Buddha to mind.
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha can cause immeasurable sins to be extinguished.
If a person mindfully recollects the Buddha,
the Buddha likewise mindfully recollects that person.
For example, just as a king’s enemies cannot harm him when he is mindful of them, so too, when one is mindful of the Buddha, unwholesome dharmas cannot cause affliction.
Some say: "The Buddha is not present in the world."
How should one recollect it?
One should have confidence that nothing surpasses wearing [it];
one should contemplate it as being like a beautiful Buddha image.
It is as if seeing the true Buddha.
First, one proceeds from the uṣṇīṣa and the hair-tuft between the brows down to the feet,
and then returns again to the mark of the uṣṇīṣa.
Having observed these characteristics with clarity, return to a quiet place;
close your eyes and reflect,
binding the mind upon the image.
Do not allow other conditions to intervene;
if other perceptions arise, withdraw them and bring them back.
Observe with your own mind, and you will see as you wish.
This is called the concentration of contemplating conditions.
One should form this thought:
"I, too, shall not go."
The image does not come;
rather, one who sees the Buddha must do so through the mind being settled and the visualization remaining stable.
Having attained the vision of the Buddha, one may then proceed to visualize the birth-body (janmakāya) and thereby see it.
It is as if facing it directly, with no difference. If the mind wanders and scatters,
frequently conditioned by unwholesome dharmas,
one should regard it like a nurse watching over her child.
If he does not refrain from committing evil,
or if his mind is unwilling to abide [in virtue],
one should immediately reprimand him, saying:
The sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death constantly press upon us.
If one is born in the heavens, one becomes attached to exquisite desires and lacks a mind for cultivation.
If one falls into the evil realms, one is terrified and distressed, and thus a virtuous mind does not arise. Now, having encountered the Buddha’s teaching—
One should recollect the Buddha with a sincere mind.
Having thus reproached oneself in various ways,
one should maintain mindfulness while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
One constantly attains the vision of the Buddha. Thereafter, one further advances to the meditative concentration of the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
Once this has been developed through successive stages, the contemplation of the birth-body becomes easy.
As for the contemplation of the Dharma (*dharmālambana*), since the mind that contemplates the image has already achieved success by following its characteristics, [the subsequent stages follow].
Immediately collecting the mind and entering meditative concentration, one will then see it;
one should contemplate the image by means of the mind.
Regarding the "contemplation of the physical body," it says:
It was as when he sat beneath the Bodhi tree,
his radiance and the marks upon his head were extraordinary;
it was also like when, in the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the five bhikṣus.
Furthermore, when Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa emits great radiance and the Buddha preaches the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma for the great assembly,
one should focus on any single point and fix the mind upon it with mindfulness.
Do not allow the mind to be distracted.
Once the mental image has become stable,
one will immediately see the Buddha.
Then his entire body experienced a bliss that permeated his four limbs,
like one who, in the heat, finds coolness, or one who, in the cold, encounters a warm chamber.
No worldly pleasure can serve as a metaphor for the Dharma-body.
As for the contemplation of the Dharma: having already seen the Buddha’s birth-body within emptiness,
one should, by means of that birth-body, contemplate the internal Dharma-body—
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great compassion, and immeasurable wholesome karma.
It is like a person who first sees a precious jewel within a golden vase;
therefore, the Dharma-body is truly wondrous,
and its divine wisdom is peerless.
There is neither near nor far;
neither difficulty nor ease.
Boundless worlds are all present before one’s eyes, such that there is not a single dharma that is not known.
There is nothing among all phenomena that is not understood.
Therefore, the practitioner should maintain focused mindfulness and not allow it to become distracted.
If the mind has other objects of focus, one should immediately withdraw it and bring it back [to the object].
Furthermore, next, all those whose lives have passed away know that at the time of death,
their various faculties first collapse as if thrown into a great pit.
They ascend as far as the Brahma Heaven,
filled with great terror;
against the boundless thief of death, only the power of the Buddha can deliver them.
They bring forth the various joys of humans, devas, and nirvana.
Furthermore, throughout all their successive lives, all Buddhas never spare their own bodies or lives for the sake of all sentient beings,
as was the case with Śākyamuni Buddha.
While he was still a crown prince, he went out on an excursion and saw a leper.
He immediately commanded his physician, saying, "One must obtain the blood of a living person for him to drink; only then will he be cured."
The Prince said, "It is difficult for such a person to find even one life; therefore, it is not right that he should die.
He then gave his own body to him so that the illness might be cured.
The Buddha acts for all sentient beings in exactly this way.
The Buddha’s kindness is deeper than that of one's parents. Suppose all people were divided into one part and two parts.
During the intervals, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha and should not harbor other thoughts.
In this way, one should perform all activities in accordance with these various meritorious recollections.
If this mindfulness is perfected, one will sever the fetters and even attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);
if one does not attain meditative concentration, one will be reborn among the six heavens of the desire realm.
This is the most honored and supreme, for one will subsequently be born before all Buddhas.
Regarding the Contemplation of Amitāyus: as for the contemplation of Amitāyus...
There are two types of persons.
One of dull faculties first contemplates an area of one inch above the forehead as being skinless and sees only the red bone;
this remains in the mind at every moment, not allowing other objects to arise.
If the mind has any other thoughts, collect them and bring them back.
Once this is accomplished,
cause the bones to transform until they are only one inch long and as white as snow.
Having done this, one is made to contemplate one's own body as entirely composed of white bones, like the color of snow.
Once this has been accomplished, one further contemplates the bones of the body.
It is the color of lapis lazuli;
its radiance is pure and clear,
penetrating through both the exterior and interior.
Having seen this,
he further caused the Vaidūrya body to emit sunbeams;
from near to far, they filled Jambudvīpa so that only light was seen.
Furthermore, he withdraws that light back into his body;
once it has completely entered, he emits it again as before.
In all meditative practices, one proceeds from the easy to the difficult.
Beginning with few and increasing to many,
once the light rays have been emitted from the body,
one should contemplate Amitābha Buddha within those rays.
That Buddha’s body emits a great radiance;
he sits facing west.
Observe his marks with careful attention.
Thereafter, one contemplates the body as a whole,
sitting in the full lotus posture like a mountain of purple gold.
Fix the attention upon this.
Do not allow other conditions to distract from the sublime marks;
if other thoughts arise, withdraw them and bring them back.
Sitting face-to-face with the Buddha, there will be no difference;
in this way, before long, you shall be able to see him. If one possesses sharp faculties, one should then contemplate [the Buddha] as being like the light of the sun.
However, one should contemplate the light of the dharma-realm as light;
by observing within that light, one will then be able to see the Buddha.
If a practitioner wishes to be reborn in the Pure Land, [they should practice thus].
One should contemplate in this manner: "I now observe the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmasatyatā*).
The world is like a dream and like an illusion, entirely devoid of reality.
It is only through inverted and false delusions that afflictions arise recklessly, leading to the experience of various retributions for transgressions."
Just as a person who sees children quarreling over tiles,
stones, wood, or earth becomes angry and distressed,
so too is it when one observes the various worlds.
One should, together with great compassion and the vow, deliver all sentient beings;
one should constantly subdue the mind and practice the two types of patience.
This refers to the patience regarding sentient beings and the patience regarding phenomena.
As for patience regarding sentient beings:
even if sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to provoke one with malicious intent.
One does not give rise to anger toward one's own lot,
nor does one give rise to joy through various forms of respect.
Furthermore, one observes sentient beings as being without priority or sequence.
If there were a prior [existence], then there would be no causal condition;
this would mean there is no beginning.
If there is no beginning, there can likewise be no middle or end.
One who contemplates in this manner does not fall into the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism;
by means of the path of peace, they contemplate all sentient beings and do not give rise to false views.
This is called the patience of sentient beings.
As for the patience regarding phenomena (dharma-kṣānti),
one should contemplate the perception that all things are ultimately empty and pure.
When the mind is free from obstruction and capable of endurance,
this is called the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*). Although those who have newly resolved their minds have not yet attained this patience of dharmas, [they should still practice it].
One should practice in this manner.
Furthermore, while contemplating the notion of the ultimate emptiness of all things,
one should constantly give rise to great compassion for sentient beings.
Whenever there is any virtuous deed, one should dedicate it all toward the aspiration to be reborn in the Land of Amitāyus Buddha.
*The Sutra on the Visualization of the Buddha*, one fascicle.
